On the outskirts of Dar es Salaam, millions of people live in sprawling informal settlements where clean water, toilets, and sewage systems can be difficult to access. Families crowd into tiny homes, children navigate open drains filled with wastewater, and something as simple as collecting drinking water can become a daily struggle. This documentary goes inside these communities to reveal the realities of life in one of Africa’s rapidly growing cities—and follows the residents trying to build a better future despite poverty, disease, and a severe lack of basic infrastructure.

Germany is one of the most important destination countries for counterfeit goods in Europe. The trade in counterfeit goods is booming—especially in clothing and accessories. But most dangerous of all are counterfeit medications.

The trade in fake medications has become extremely lucrative. In some cases, it is even more profitable than the drug trade. This investigative documentary traces the paths of counterfeit brand-name products and medications, uncovers production facilities, and exposes the criminal networks behind them.

Each year, a train carrying doctors and medical gear travels through remote areas of Kazakhstan. The project is called Salamatty Kazakhstan, or "Healthy Kazakhstan." The train is underway for eight months and the clinic operates daily.

Salamatty Kazakhstan was launched by the government to improve medical care in the country's sparsely populated regions. Some communities are hundreds of kilometers from the nearest hospital or clinic. The train's timetable is shared online.

In addition to medical staff, the train crew includes kitchen staff, stewards, and technicians. On its journey of around 20,000 kilometers, the train stops in numerous villages and small towns in the Kazakh countryside. Forcing society to think, the story of Dekh Tamasha Dekh, Kya Munna Kya Muniya, narrates the pain of having a girl. Society celebrates the birth of a boy, but the birth of a girl brings mourning to the family, the village, and society. A boy's birth opens the door to heaven, but the birth of a girl closes it. Why aren't girls given the same freedom as boys? A mother never discriminates between the children born from her womb, yet in the eyes of her family, she is considered guilty. The story seems to convey this narrow-mindedness.

In Jeju Province, located off the southern coast of Korea, are the women of the sea who hold the breath of life. Typhoons and the barren volcanic soil of the islands left the people enduring years of poor harvests and famine. For survival, women looked to the frigid sea. Haenyeos, women of the sea, still exist, and they have been diving without air tanks for more than 1,000 years. They go into waters 10 to 20 meters deep to harvest seaweed and shellfish to make a living. They work from 7 to 8 hours a day without even a sip of fresh water. At the end of the day, they return with sumbisori, a whale-like noise at the end of their breath.
